note: No source dates the start of Sogmatar as a site. English Wikipedia only reports that a series of Syriac inscriptions dating to the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE have been found there, which dates the inscriptions and not the construction, foundation or first occupation of the site, and the Iron Age and 3,000-year-old statements in the news reports are period words or worked-out ages. The field stays empty and the site goes to the owner's list.

No page found prints a point for the Axura necropolises themselves: the Wikipedia articles (en, az, tr) and Wikidata carry none, and the only coordinates available are those of Axura village, which is not the site.

The Wikipedia article dates the three necropolises inconsistently (end of the Iron Age, the III-VIII centuries, the first centuries AD, the 14th-18th centuries) with no single start stated in a century with that word; a period word alone does not date the site.

The cultural inventory page for the Hierapolis Frontinus gate describes the monument in prose and gives its date, but prints no coordinates, and no other readable source gives a point for this north gate. The stored point therefore stays unsourced and the site goes to the owner's list.

No source dates the start of Yanaca. The English article says it is extremely difficult to know when the first inhabitants arrived and that the first settlers probably arrived around 2,000 BCE, but that figure is explicitly attributed to archaeological studies at other sites in the area of Pacaicasa (Ayacucho), not to Yanaca itself, so it cannot be read as a start year for this site. The field stays empty.
Wikipedia only says the road is often associated with the Roman Empire and may have predated the Roman occupation; no source gives a year, century or millennium for its start.

No readable source prints a point for the Roman aqueduct of Constantine: its Wikidata item Q122114787 and Commons category carry none, French Wikipedia (Constantine, Cirta) gives none, Harba-DZ and Mapcarta show no coordinates as text.
No readable source gives a year or century for the start of this aqueduct; Harba-DZ calls it only antique, Wikipedia only Roman.

The article says the name is first mentioned on a milestone of 45/46 AD and the Antalya culture directorate states that no evidence for a Hellenistic or earlier Trebenna has been found, but no source gives a construction or foundation year for the city itself.
Sources only give period words (Early Classic stela, Classic kingdom of Hixwitz, 7th century eclipse by Zapote Bobal), no start year or century for the site's foundation or first occupation.
Wikipedia gives no date for the Corick stone circle and row; no readable source dates the site's start.

No readable page prints a point for the Via degli Inferi itself: Wikipedia has no article, Commons/Wikidata have no item, the Etruskey and Cerveteri pages print none, and Wikipedia's point for the Banditaccia necropolis is for the necropolis centre, about 1.7 km from the stored point.

Readable pages only date tombs and road works along the road (tumuli from the 6th century BC on the main sepulchral road, tombs and a road inscription of the 4th century BC); none states when the Via degli Inferi itself was made.

The site is Tabuco (Tubuco), the pre-Hispanic Tuxpan on the right bank of the Tuxpan river mouth, Veracruz; no readable source printing a coordinate pair for it was found (only the Megalithic Portal gives the stored point).
Spanish sources call Tabuco a small ceremonial centre and the first settlement of Tuxpan, but no readable source gives an English word of a canonical type; the field stays empty.

site_name: Tempio Nuragico a Pozzo di Irru
note: The pages on the Irru complex (La Sardegna verso l'Unesco, Wikipedia on Nulvi, the list of Nuragic holy wells) describe the well temple without any date, and the only dates are for Nuragic wells as a class.

Neither Wikipedia (en, pt) nor its Wikidata item gives coordinates, and the Ministry of Culture resolution of 2025 only refers to a perimeter plan; the only point found (a Mapcarta/OSM node) lies at Huaytara town beside its Plaza de Armas, while MINCETUR places the ruins about 3 km north of Huaytara, so no sourced point for the site itself exists.
Wikipedia and the MINCETUR inventory entry give no date for Runayoc; the resolution of 2025 concerns protection, not dating.

The German Wikipedia article on the Karasis fortress prints its coordinates only in German notation (37°33'8" N, 35°51'57" O, with O for Ost), and no readable source states the point in a form I can quote, so the stored point stays unsourced.

site_name: Cras -  Round Cairn to North of
note: The register and the Welsh article about this cairn place it after the end of the Stone Age and at the beginning of the Bronze Age, and the scheduled monument list calls its period 'Prehistoric'. That is a period, not a year, century or millennium for the start of the cairn.

English Wikipedia dates only the 16th-17th century documents about the estate and says the Punic tombs and Late Roman-Byzantine catacombs were found there, without giving a start date for the site; a period word or the date of a document is not a start date.

Neither Wikipedia nor Wikidata gives a point for Venado Beach (Playa Venado, near the Venado River mouth, Pacific coast of Panama), and no readable page for this site prints coordinates; map pages found are about namesake beaches elsewhere in Panama.

Wikipedia and the excavation reports (Chaluleu 2019, Reyes et al. 2019) date the first occupation only as Late Preclassic, a period word without year, century or millennium; no readable source gives a dated start.

No source I could read prints a point for the Al-Sanea tomb itself. The Arabic Wikipedia article that served as the stored source_url no longer exists, the coordinates on offer (English Wikipedia, Danish Wikipedia, ancientlocations.net) are the point of the whole of Hegra/Mada'in Salih and not of the tomb, and the brief bars a namesake or region point. The stored point therefore stays for the owner.

No readable source prints a point for Nina Kiru/Ninaquero; Wikipedia and Wikidata give none, the MINCETUR record gives no coordinates, and the stored point is the generic Lucanas province centroid, far from Andamarca.
MINCETUR assigns the mausoleum only to the Late Horizon (Inca) period, a period word without a year or century; no source dates the start.

English and Macedonian Wikipedia and the E-Tour Guide page only give a period word (late antiquity) and the general importance of the Balkan provinces towards the close of the 3rd and the 4th century AD; none dates the foundation or first occupation of this fortification.

The only printed points (Wikipedia/Wikidata 17.42, -89.67) lie about 38 km from the stored point and do not fit the article's own description (7 km north-east of El Zotz, 20 km west of Tikal); no readable source prints a point for the site itself.

Wikipedia dates the site to the second half of the 4th century AD, but the excavators (Garrison et al. 2016) place its establishment as a sacred hilltop site in the Late Preclassic (400 BC-AD 250), a range spanning two buckets, and their abstract is not readable by plain GET; no consistent start can be quoted.

The English Wikipedia article says the Cotzumalhuapa zone dates mainly to the Late Classic period, was occupied since the Middle Preclassic period, and holds monuments ranging from Pre-Classic to the Late Classic (600-1000 CE). These are period words and a range for the monuments of the zone, not a year a source gives for its start.

No readable page prints a point for the Haidara monument at Qab Elias; the listed articles give none, and the only nearby point found is OpenStreetMap's node as JSON, which cannot be quoted as page text.
L'Orient Today only places Haidara in the Roman period (Roman religious and funerary purposes) without a year or century for its construction, so no start can be quoted.

The only point I can quote for Kerbatch is the French Wikipedia infobox coordinate 13° 45′ nord, 15° 06′ ouest, which lies about 3.4 km from the stored point and is given to whole arcminutes for a 0.79 ha group of nine cromlechs; Wikidata carries the same point, imported from that article, so it is not a second witness. No readable source places the circles themselves at the stored point, so the stored point stays and the question goes to the owner.
No source I read dates the Founder's House itself; the Roman type of the villa is a period description, not a year, century or millennium for its construction.
No page about the Founder's House itself was found; the pages that name it, the ToposText gazetteer entry and the Turkish museum page, are entries for the city of Termessos as a whole.
The article dates the finds from the Mesolithic only as 11,000-7,000 BP, a BP range for a whole forest of sites of many periods; no source gives a start year for this entry.
The English Wikipedia article only places the site on a mountain of the same name in the San Cristobal District, near Puka Urqu, and gives no year, century or millennium for its start.

Livius, Wikipedia and the other readable pages print no point for the Qasr Naous temples; the Ain Akrine Wikipedia point is that of the village (about 0.4 km from the stored point), not of the temples on the hill, so no source gives the site's own point.
Livius calls the two temples Roman and says only that the settlement north of them seems quite late; no readable source gives a year or century for their construction.
Wikipedia only calls the site prehistoric and The Northern Antiquarian pages on the circle and the necropolis give no date or period for it; no source dates the start.
